snapshot.title: TNPSC History: National Renaissance
snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ TNPSC GS Hook: Ram Mohan: Sati 1829. Adyar: Theosophical. Dayanand: Vedas. 1893: Chicago. 1897: RK Mission.

quick_notes.title: Brahmo Samaj
quick_notes.detail: Raja Ram Mohan Roy (1828). "Father of Modern India". Sati abolition (1829).
quick_notes.explanation: The Brahmo Samaj was a religious and social reform movement started in 1828 by Raja Ram Mohan Roy, who is called the "Father of Modern India" because he worked to bring modern ideas like reason and equality into Indian society. "Sati" was a custom where a widow was forced to burn alive on her husband's funeral pyre; Raja Ram Mohan Roy strongly opposed it, and in 1829 the British government passed a law banning the practice, which is known as the abolition of Sati. The Brahmo Samaj believed in one God, rejected idol worship, and fought for women's rights and education. This movement helped start modern social reforms in India.

quick_notes.title: Arya Samaj
quick_notes.detail: Dayanand Saraswati (1875). "Go back to Vedas". Slogan : "India for Indians".
quick_notes.explanation: Arya Samaj is a Hindu reform movement founded by Dayanand Saraswati in the year 1875. Dayanand Saraswati taught that people should reject later additions to Hinduism and instead "go back to the Vedas," which are the oldest sacred scriptures of Hinduism. He believed the Vedas contained pure, original knowledge and that all social and religious practices should be based on them. The movement also promoted the slogan "India for Indians," meaning that India should be governed by its own people and not by foreign rulers like the British. This idea helped inspire a sense of national pride and self-rule among Indians.

quick_notes.title: Theosophical Society
quick_notes.detail: Founded by Blavatsky and Olcott (USA). Shifted to Adyar, Madras (1882). Popularized by Annie Besant.
quick_notes.explanation: The Theosophical Society is a group that explores spiritual wisdom, mysticism, and the common truths behind all religions. It was founded in the United States by Helena Blavatsky and Henry Steel Olcott. In 1882, the society moved its headquarters to Adyar, a neighborhood in Madras (now Chennai), India. Annie Besant, a British social reformer, later joined the society and helped make it widely known in India.

quick_notes.title: Ramakrishna Mission
quick_notes.detail: Swami Vivekananda (1897). Chicago speech (1893). Service to humanity.
quick_notes.explanation: Ramakrishna Mission (1897) is a religious and social service organization founded by Swami Vivekananda, who was the chief disciple of the saint Ramakrishna Paramahamsa. Four years earlier, in 1893, Vivekananda gave a famous speech at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago, USA, where he introduced Hinduism and called for universal tolerance. The mission's core teaching is that serving people in need—such as the poor, sick, or uneducated—is the same as serving God, because God lives in every human being. It does not try to convert anyone to a new religion, but instead works to help people improve their lives through education, healthcare, and disaster relief while staying true to their own faith. The headquarters of the Mission is in Belur Math, West Bengal, and it operates schools, hospitals, libraries, and rural development projects across India and other countries.

quick_notes.title: Prarthana Samaj
quick_notes.detail: Atmaram Pandurang (1867). Social reform in Maharashtra.
quick_notes.explanation: Prarthana Samaj was a social reform movement founded in 1867 in Maharashtra by Atmaram Pandurang. The word "Prarthana Samaj" means "Prayer Society" in English, and it focused on reforming Hindu society by promoting the worship of one God without idols, and by opposing caste discrimination and the practice of untouchability. The Samaj believed in reason and social justice, and it worked to improve the status of women by supporting widow remarriage and women's education. Unlike some other reform groups, the Prarthana Samaj did not break away from Hinduism but tried to reform it from within, using prayer meetings and public discussions to spread its ideas. Its members, including famous reformers like Mahadev Govind Ranade and R.G. Bhandarkar, also campaigned against child marriage and the rigid caste system. Through these efforts, the Prarthana Samaj became an important part of the broader social reform movement in 19th-century India.
